label: The Group of Symplectomorphisms
notes: This chapter, printed pages 385 to 416, treats the diffeomorphisms preserving a symplectic form as an infinite-dimensional Lie group. We meet the full group, its identity component, the Hamiltonian subgroup, and two homomorphisms, flux and Calabi, that measure exactly how a path fails to be Hamiltonian.

label: Symp and Its Identity Component
notes: Symplectomorphisms form a group under composition because preserving omega is closed under inverses and products. The identity component collects those reachable by a continuous path from the identity. Distinguishing the whole group from this component already records topological information about the manifold and its symmetries.

label: The Lie Algebra of Symp
notes: Differentiating a symplectic isotopy gives a vector field whose contraction with omega is a closed one-form. So the Lie algebra of the symplectomorphism group is the symplectic vector fields, identified with closed one-forms. Hamiltonian fields correspond to exact one-forms, the differentials of functions.

label: Hamiltonian Symplectomorphisms
notes: A Hamiltonian symplectomorphism is the time-one map of a flow generated by a time-dependent function. These maps form a normal subgroup Ham inside the identity component. The generating Hamiltonian is the central computational object: its flow preserves the form and, on closed manifolds, conserves nothing extra by accident.

label: Symplectic versus Hamiltonian Fields
notes: Every Hamiltonian field is symplectic, but the converse fails when the first cohomology is nontrivial. The obstruction is precisely whether the closed one-form i_X omega is exact. On a torus a constant translation field is symplectic yet not Hamiltonian, which is the simplest visible gap.

label: The Flux Homomorphism
notes: Flux assigns to a symplectic isotopy the cohomology class obtained by integrating the one-forms of its generating fields over time. It descends to a homomorphism from the identity component into the first cohomology modulo a period lattice Gamma, measuring the swept class accumulated along the path.

label: Flux of a Loop
notes: For a loop of symplectomorphisms the flux integral pairs against each one-cycle, recording the signed area swept as the cycle is dragged around the loop. The period subgroup Gamma is exactly the set of flux values of loops, which is why the quotient is the right target.

label: Ham as the Kernel of Flux
notes: The flux homomorphism fits into a short exact sequence whose kernel is the Hamiltonian group. So an isotopy is Hamiltonian if and only if its flux vanishes. This identifies Ham as a kernel, gives it a normal-subgroup structure, and frames the flux conjecture about discreteness of Gamma.

label: The Calabi Homomorphism
notes: On an exact symplectic manifold the compactly supported Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms admit a further homomorphism, Calabi, integrating the generating Hamiltonian against the volume form over time. It is well defined independent of the chosen generating path and provides a nontrivial real-valued invariant of the group.

label: Calabi as a Volume Integral
notes: Calabi averages the Hamiltonian over phase space and over the time interval, producing a single real number. Because admissible reparametrizations and conjugations leave this average unchanged, the construction is a genuine homomorphism whose kernel is a simple group in many cases of interest.

label: Topology of the Group
notes: The homotopy type of the symplectomorphism group carries deep geometry. Gromov computed it for the four-ball and the product of spheres, finding it deformation retracts onto a familiar compact Lie group. Such results connect group topology to pseudoholomorphic curve methods developed later in the book.

label: The Tower and Exact Sequence
notes: We close with the structural picture: Hamiltonian inside identity component inside full group, threaded by the flux exact sequence and, in exact settings, the Calabi homomorphism on compactly supported maps. This tower organizes every invariant of the chapter into one diagram worth memorizing.
